items.proposition: The supplied Delhi statutory materials make post-9 June 1952 subletting, assignment, or other parting with possession a section 14(1)(b) eviction ground when done without the landlord's consent in writing; the supplied section 16 additionally states that, after commencement of the Act, a tenant may not transfer or assign tenancy rights without the landlord's previous consent in writing.

evidence.quote: that the tenant has, on or after the 9th day of June, 1952, sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord;

After the commencement of this Act, no tenant shall, without the previous consent in writing of the landlord, -(a) sub-let the whole or any part of the premises held by him as a tenant; or(b) transfer or assign his rights in the tenancy or in any part thereof.

items.relevance: These are the most direct supplied statutory candidates for the fixed ground and make the existence and legal sufficiency of written consent central once a qualifying transfer or parting with possession is shown.
items.limits: Both statutory units are supplied as Indian Kanoon reproductions whose historical version is expressly unverified rather than authenticated historical consolidations. Section 16 supplies related statutory context but the fixed eviction ground is section 14(1)(b).
items.review_reason: One model-assisted review of original unit text confirms the stated proposition and limited role. The Delhi statute is a version-limited reproduction; GR reported Delhi is a report of precedent, not its full opinion. For bank succession, TS remains prima facie/reserved and GR an AP-law analogy, not a Delhi holding. Unlocated model quotation strings are retained as quotation defects; reviewer anchors below point to the unaltered source, not a silently repaired quotation.

items.proposition: The allowed target record states that in 1959 Allen Berry & Co. transferred or assigned the tenancy to the appellant and put the appellant in possession, including a specific statement that possession of the whole premises was parted with.

evidence.quote: Sometime in 1959 Allen Berry & Co. transferred the lease to the appellant and put the latter in possession.
In or about May, 1959, the tenant assigned the tenancy rights.
and parted with possession of the whole of the premises to the appellant.

items.relevance: If these allowed-record statements are used as the factual premise, they directly correspond to the statutory alternatives of assignment and parting with possession, and the stated 1959 timing is after 9 June 1952.
items.limits: The supplied record does not include the complete transfer instrument or all underlying evidence concerning the transaction. This proposition identifies the allowed-record characterization and does not infer the withheld final adjudication.
items.review_reason: Contains target-record IDs rather than an all-library legal-source bundle. Retained as qualitative analysis, not converted into invented legal units or a legal retrieval denominator.

items.proposition: The appellant's supplied written-consent position is that clause 7 of the original lease itself constituted the landlords' written consent to assignment because the lease's definition of the lessee included assigns.

evidence.quote: Counsel for the appellant submitted that by cl. 7 of the lease, the landlords have given their consent in writing to the assignment.
the expression "THE LESSEE" hereinbefore used' shall include their representatives and assigns.

items.relevance: This is the principal supplied material bearing on the statutory written-consent element; if the clause legally amounts to consent to assignment, that would materially affect whether the section 14(1)(b) condition is met.
items.limits: The allowed record presents this as the appellant's contention and supplies the clause wording, but does not supply the target court's resolution of whether this definitional language legally constitutes the required consent in writing. The complete lease and any additional assignment restrictions or permissions are not supplied.

items.proposition: A later Supreme Court source reports Parasaram Harnand Rao as construing Delhi section 14(b) broadly enough to cover sublease, assignment, any other mode of parting with possession, and even involuntary sale.

evidence.quote: This Court held that the amplitude of S. 14(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act was wide enough not only to include any sublease but even an assignment or any other mode by which possession of the tenanted premises is parted.
In view of the wide amplitude of s. 14(b), it does not exclude even an involuntary sale.

items.relevance: The reported interpretation supports treating an assignment or other transfer of possession as falling within the type of conduct addressed by section 14(1)(b), rather than limiting the provision to conventional subleases.
items.limits: The supplied unit is from a Supreme Court judgment dated 17 April 1986 reporting the earlier Parasaram decision; the Parasaram opinion itself is not independently supplied. It therefore has the status of a reported precedent in this library, and it post-dates the 19 April 1965 target case, so it cannot be treated as evidence of the target court's historical reasoning.

items.proposition: In a 1980 Delhi High Court company-amalgamation setting, the supplied source stated only prima facie that court-ordered vesting of tenancy rights on amalgamation might not require landlord consent and might fall outside section 14(1)(b), while expressly reserving the eviction issue and preserving any landlord remedy if the transaction amounted to an assignment in law.

evidence.quote: Prima facie, the rights of the transferor-company in the tenancy, contractual or statutory, are transferable on an amalgamation by virtue of the vesting order to be made by the court while sanctioning the scheme of amalgamation or thereafter and having regard to the nature of such a vesting it would not require the consent of the landlord and would be outside the mischief of the provisions of s. 14(1)(b) of the Rent Control Act.

This court is, however, not concerned at this stage if the transfer by or consequent on amalgamation by the order of the court would nevertheless be tantamount to the assignment of a tenancy and if without the consent of the landlord would render the company or the transferee-company liable to eviction under s. 14(1)(b) of the Rent Control Act or otherwise be actionable in a regular civil action against them.

If there is any assignment in law, which may attract the provisions of the Delhi Rent Control Act, the landlord would be free to take recourse to the proceedings under that Act or in a regular civil action and such proceedings would be dealt with and decided by the appropriate authority in accordance with law.

items.relevance: This is a potentially opposing Delhi-law analogy where possession or tenancy rights move through a court-sanctioned corporate vesting rather than an ordinary voluntary assignment.
items.limits: The source is a Delhi High Court decision dated 5 December 1980, is expressly marked prima facie and reserved, and concerns amalgamation and a vesting order. The allowed target record supplies no comparable amalgamation or court-ordered vesting facts, so the analogy is limited.
items.review_reason: Main proposition is supported with the recorded scope limits, but its inclusion as a useful legal reference for this non-amalgamation target is disputable. Full source/quotation defects retained; exclude from primary denominator and include symmetrically in sensitivity analysis.

items.proposition: In a later adopted Supreme Court application under the Andhra Pradesh rent statute, a company-proposed court-sanctioned amalgamation was treated as a transfer rather than an involuntary transfer immune from rent-control consequences, and the absence of written landlord consent was treated as material.

evidence.quote: As such it cannot be said that this is an involuntary transfer effected by order of the court.
There is undoubtedly no written permission or consent of the respondent landlord to this transfer of tenancy right of the 1st appellant company as required under S. 10(ii)(a) of the said Act.

There is no express provision in the said Act that in case of any involuntary transfer or transfer of the tenancy right by virtue of a scheme of amalgamation sanctioned by the court by its order under ss. 391 and 394 of the Companies Act as in the present case, such transfer will not come within the purview of S. 10(ii)(a) of the said Act.

items.relevance: This provides a contrasting adopted treatment of a corporate-transfer argument and cautions against assuming that every court-sanctioned transfer is automatically exempt from rent-control restrictions.
items.limits: The source is a Supreme Court decision dated 17 April 1986 applying the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act and a particular lease clause, not Delhi section 14(1)(b). It post-dates the target and is only an analogy; it cannot supply the governing Delhi rule for this 1965 record.
items.review_reason: Main proposition is supported with the recorded scope limits, but its inclusion as a useful legal reference for this non-amalgamation target is disputable. Full source/quotation defects retained; exclude from primary denominator and include symmetrically in sensitivity analysis.

analysis_points: On the supplied materials, the statutory conduct and timing components have direct record support: section 14(1)(b) expressly identifies assignment and other parting with possession after 9 June 1952, while the allowed record describes a 1959 assignment and transfer of possession of the whole premises. This supplies substantial support for the fixed eviction ground subject to the written-consent issue.

Written consent is the central unresolved issue in the allowed target record. The appellant expressly relies on clause 7, particularly the inclusion of "assigns" within the definition of "THE LESSEE", but no supplied target unit decides whether that wording is an authorization to assign or merely definitional language.

The later reported Parasaram interpretation supports a broad reading of section 14(b) covering assignment and other modes of parting with possession, including involuntary sale. Its value here is interpretive support only: the underlying Parasaram opinion is not independently supplied and the reporting source post-dates the target case.

The amalgamation materials should be kept secondary. Telesound offers only a prima facie, expressly reserved Delhi view that certain court-ordered vesting may not require consent, while General Radio later reaches a different adopted result under Andhra Pradesh law. The target record does not show that its 1959 assignment resulted from any comparable statutory or court-sanctioned amalgamation.

The source-grounded position therefore supports the section 14(1)(b) ground on assignment/parting-with-possession facts if the required written consent was absent, but the supplied materials do not permit a reference constructor to resolve the legal sufficiency of clause 7 or to infer the withheld historical final outcome.
gaps: The complete 1956 lease is not supplied; only the clause relied on for the consent argument is reproduced, so any other restriction, permission, qualification, or contextual language concerning assignment is unknown.

No separate landlord consent letter, endorsement, assignment instrument, or other writing evidencing consent is supplied, and the record does not provide additional evidence resolving whether the landlords affirmatively authorized this particular 1959 assignment.

The Delhi statutory texts are supplied as present Indian Kanoon reproductions with historical-version verification expressly unresolved; an authenticated consolidation establishing the exact operative historical text and commencement context for 1959 is not supplied.
The full Parasaram opinion is not in the library; only a later Supreme Court judgment's report of that precedent is supplied.

The allowed scope expressly excludes the target final reasoning and outcome, so those withheld materials cannot be used to settle the consent dispute or reconstruct the historical disposition.

disputes: Whether clause 7's statement that "THE LESSEE" includes representatives and assigns constitutes the landlord's statutorily sufficient consent in writing to assignment, as the appellant contends, or merely defines who falls within contractual terminology; the supplied target record does not resolve that question.

How much weight to give the later reported Parasaram interpretation when constructing a reference for a 1965 target: it directly concerns Delhi section 14(b) and supports breadth, but the underlying opinion is not supplied and the reporting judgment is later.

Whether company-amalgamation authorities have any meaningful application to this record. Telesound's potentially favorable no-consent view was prima facie and expressly reserved, General Radio's contrary treatment was adopted under Andhra Pradesh law, and the allowed target record contains no amalgamation or statutory-vesting facts.
